summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans and gender-nonconforming visitors, and the state provides no protection machinery when that danger materialises.

No legal provision prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A visitor refused service, assaulted or turned away by police has no statutory basis for a complaint, according to the US State Department's 2023 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices.

The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman, and same-sex marriage is banned. A visitor travelling with a partner therefore arrives with no recognised relationship, and affection between same-sex partners in public falls within reach of the public-morals provisions.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A trans traveller whose documents do not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at border control and at police stops, and nothing in the sources indicates that any authority treats an incongruent document as settled.

Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not explicitly criminalised in the penal code. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and same-sex conduct in public draws harsher penalties than other offences covered by the same moral-offence provisions. The practical effect for a visitor is that visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct in public exposes them to arrest on morals grounds.

Criminalisation of same-sex activity in public has pushed the community underground, and no organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights are known to operate in the country. A visitor who is detained or assaulted has no domestic advocacy body to turn to, and approaching the authorities carries the risk of identifying oneself under the same morals provisions.

Attitudes toward sexual orientation and gender identity remain taboo and are widely framed as imported from Europe and contrary to African values. That framing shapes both the likelihood of hostile encounters in public and the response a visitor can expect from bystanders and police.
tangentialFactors:
The Central African Republic appears in ILGA World's 2023 survey Our Identities Under Arrest, which documents laws criminalising LGBT people across jurisdictions, including states that reach same-sex conduct through general morals provisions rather than explicit statutory bans.

The 2012 US State Department human rights report for the Central African Republic records extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, alongside harsh prison conditions. The report contains little LGBT-specific material, but it establishes the conditions any visitor of any background would face after an arrest.

The country has received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations concerning sexual orientation and gender identity, covering non-discrimination and the situation of sexual minorities. Stakeholder submissions to the 45th session of the review in January 2024, summarised by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, again included SOGI-related recommendations. These recommendations are advisory, and no source in the inventory documents legislative change following either cycle.
localsOnly:
LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the Central African Republic's military, a restriction that binds residents and citizens rather than visitors, per the US State Department's 2023 report.

With legal gender recognition unavailable, residents have no route to amend the sex marker on identity documents, so national identity papers and official records continue to carry the marker originally assigned.

Residents who partner with a same-sex person hold no marital or partnership recognition, and public expression of that relationship is exposed to prosecution under Article 85 of the penal code.

No organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights are known to be operating domestically, leaving residents without a local body for legal advocacy, public campaigning or shelter, and pushing support-seeking onto external contacts.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific penalties attached to Article 85, including fine levels and terms of imprisonment, are not stated in the sources supplied for this record.

No arrest or prosecution figures for public-morals offences are available in the inventory, so how often Article 85 is enforced against same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct remains unresolved.

Whether gender-nonconforming presentation alone, without accompanying same-sex conduct, is sufficient to trigger arrest is not documented. The treatment of visitors whose travel documents do not match their presentation is likewise not sourced.

The 2012 US State Department report contains little LGBT-specific material, and no source in the inventory covers hate-motivated violence against trans visitors in the years between that report and the 2023 report. Whether assaults motivated by gender identity qualify as hate crimes or attract enhanced penalties is also unsourced.

The January 2024 stakeholder submissions to the Universal Periodic Review are summarised rather than reproduced, so the individual recommendations addressed to the Central African Republic and any government response to them remain unresolved.
